claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight HEA is in a nonequilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
Controlled thermal aging promotes the evolution of chemical short-range order in the alloy.
Chemical short-range order preferentially drives nucleation of Mg-containing intermetallic phases.
The resulting transformation modifies the alloy's surface chemistry.
The resulting transformation modifies the alloy's defect structure.
Changes in surface chemistry and defect structure alter corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Manufacturing processes can create nonequilibrium SRO states distinct from equilibrium SRO states.
Thermally activated nonequilibrium SRO is a kinetic precursor that triggers intermetallic phase formation.
Mg-containing intermetallic precipitates alter the alloy's ability to form protective oxide scales and passivating films.
Thermally aged material will contain dispersed fine intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries or within the matrix.
Intermetallics that promote beneficial passivation will permit retention of corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Excessive or coarsened intermetallics will disrupt surface-layer integrity and degrade corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Moderate aging below approximately 600 degrees Celsius initiates SRO evolution and intermetallic nucleation.
Above approximately 600 degrees Celsius, intermetallic phase stability critically affects oxidation performance.
The kinetics of SRO evolution and intermetallic nucleation are sensitive to small variations in composition and thermal history.
Precipitate size distribution and spatial arrangement depend on alloy composition and thermal history.
The controlled comparison is between samples retained in the initial metastable state and thermally aged samples.
